vignette:
She is 52, a South Eastern Asian woman who has spent most of her adult life working as a librarian, someone who once took comfort in order, quiet, and the reliable placement of things. Before the disaster, she describes her life in small, steady routines: opening the library in the morning, running her fingers along the spines of returned books, helping schoolchildren find stories, going home to her husband in the evening to cook rice and soup and watch television together. She is not someone who had thought of herself as easily shaken. She says she used to be “the calm one” in her family.

The storm changes that. It arrives after days of warnings that become background noise, the kind people half-believe because storms come every year. She remembers the air feeling strange, heavy and metallic, and the way neighbors move with forced cheerfulness as they tie things down and stack supplies. When the water starts rising, it rises faster than she thinks is possible. By the time she and her husband realize they need to leave, the road is already filling. She remembers the sound most vividly: wind slamming debris against walls, glass breaking somewhere nearby, people shouting over one another, and underneath it all the rushing water, relentless and alive.

They try to move to higher ground with a few belongings in plastic bags. At one point the current nearly pulls her off her feet. She feels her husband’s hand clamp around her wrist so tightly it leaves marks for days. She sees a motorbike tip and disappear, sees a woman screaming for someone she cannot reach, sees a dog carried away. For hours afterward, time loses sequence. She remembers standing in a crowded shelter soaked through, shivering despite the heat, unable to stop staring at the doorway as if the water might enter there too. She does not sleep that night or the next. Even after they are physically safe, her body acts as if the danger is still moving toward her.

In the weeks after, she tells herself she is fortunate. She and her husband survive. Their home is damaged but not destroyed. At the library, many books are ruined, their pages swollen and warped, and she finds herself unexpectedly close to tears while sorting them into discard piles. She is embarrassed by how much this affects her. Other people have lost relatives, entire houses. She keeps saying, “We are lucky,” but the words feel disconnected from the fear that continues inside her.

As the months pass, she waits to return to normal and becomes frightened when she does not. Rain, even light rain on the roof, makes her chest tighten. When dark clouds gather, she begins checking weather updates repeatedly, sometimes every few minutes, unable to stop herself. At night she lies awake listening for wind. If she does fall asleep, she often wakes abruptly from dreams in which water is rising through the floorboards or she is trying to run while carrying books that dissolve in her arms. Her husband tells her she cries out in her sleep. Sometimes she wakes disoriented, heart pounding, and for a moment does not know whether she is in the shelter again.

At work she is still efficient, but only from the outside. She startles when carts bang into shelves or when children drop books. During the rainy season, she avoids the windows and asks coworkers to handle anything involving the basement archive because she cannot bear going downstairs. She used to enjoy helping with library events, especially crowded community programs, but now she positions herself near exits and scans the room without realizing it. If a patron lingers too long talking about the weather or flooding in another province, she feels her throat close and has to excuse herself to the staff room. There she stands very still, pressing her palms against the table until the feeling passes.

Her world gradually narrows. She no longer visits friends during monsoon months unless her husband drives and promises to leave early. She keeps important documents in sealed bags by the front door. She has packed an emergency kit three separate times, each one more elaborate than the last. Her husband first responds gently, then with frustration, telling her they are prepared, that she is safe now. She knows he is trying to help, but when he says “safe” she feels something in her harden. Safe feels like a word for other people.

What troubles her most is how changed she feels from the woman she was before. In the library, she catches herself reshelving the same cart twice because she cannot remember where she placed books moments earlier. She avoids the local history section because there is a display on regional typhoons. She feels ashamed of her irritability, of snapping at patrons for minor things, of resenting children for laughing loudly when she used to enjoy their noise. Sometimes she sits in her car after work with her hands on the steering wheel, too exhausted to drive, watching the sky and calculating how quickly water could rise on the street.

She still goes to work, still cooks dinner, still folds her husband’s shirts and answers neighbors politely. From the outside, her life appears intact. But she lives as if the storm has not ended, as if some part of her remains standing in dirty water, listening for the next sound that means she has only seconds left to run.
